title: You realize mid-sprint that your estimate was wrong and the feature won't ship on time. What do you do?
description: Surfacing bad news early without drama: re-estimate with evidence, present options instead of excuses, cut scope deliberately, and fix the estimation process afterward.

data.text: **Question:** You realize mid-sprint that your estimate was wrong and the feature won't ship on time. What do you do?

Raise it immediately — the same day you know — with evidence, not apologies: what you've learned since the estimate, where the remaining work actually is, and two or three options with trade-offs (cut scope, extend the date, get help, or descope to a walk-behind release). Never silently absorb the slip until the deadline arrives; a surprise at the deadline is a management failure, a signal at mid-sprint is engineering working as intended. Afterward, close the loop on *why* the estimate missed so the next one is better.

**Step 1 — Re-estimate with today's information.** Estimates are predictions made under ignorance; when the ignorance resolves, the estimate changes. Be concrete: 'the schema migration needs an expand-and-contract pass — 3 days, not 1. The API work itself is done.'

**Step 2 — Surface early, with options.** Go to your lead/PM with: the new number, the reason in one sentence, and options:
- **Cut scope**: ship the core flow now, the polish items next sprint (usually the best option)
- **Extend**: only if there's a genuine external reason; state the new date firmly
- **Add capacity**: note that adding people late to software often costs more than it saves — offer it honestly
- **Ship behind a flag**: deliver code safely, enable when ready

**Step 3 — Protect the team's credibility.** 'I underestimated X because we discovered Y' is professional; hiding it or working silent nights to 'make it up' trains the team that estimates are promises — which guarantees future surprises.

**Step 4 — Fix the process, not the person.** Retrospective item: was the unknown a spike-able risk? Should the story have been split smaller? Did we estimate without touching the scariest file? Common fixes: timebox an investigation spike before estimating, split stories until each is ≤2 days, and add explicit buffers for integration work.

**What interviewers are really probing:** integrity under pressure, communication comfort with superiors, and whether you treat estimates as contracts or as feedback.

data.title: The one-sentence framing that lands
data.text: "I'm at risk of missing Friday — I've re-scoped, and here are three options with trade-offs." It shows ownership, analysis, and respect for the other person's decision, all at once.

Interviewers assess:
- Early escalation — the opposite of heroically hiding it
- Options with trade-offs instead of a bare 'I can't make it'
- Honesty about what changed the estimate
- A concrete step to improve future estimates (spikes, smaller splits)

items: Waiting until the deadline to reveal the slip — the only truly unforgivable option
Presenting problems without options and pushing the decision entirely upward
Blaming the requirements or another team instead of re-estimating
Heroic weekend work that burns you out and hides the estimation problem
Never following up on why the estimate was wrong — so it happens again
How do you handle a manager who rejects all three options and demands the original date?
What estimation techniques (planning poker, t-shirt, reference class) do you use?
How do you split a story so estimates become reliable?
When is a spike the right tool before estimating?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Re-estimate with current knowledge, then escalate the same day
Bring options (cut scope / extend / flag it), not just bad news
Treat estimates as forecasts, not contracts — surprises are the failure
Retro the cause: spikes, smaller splits, buffer on integration work
data.takeaway: Bad news early is management information; bad news on deadline day is a broken promise.
